Why Don’t We Track What We Believed? Johndineshgku 8 min read · Sep 21, 2026 -- Listen Share Product teams have systems for delivery, analytics and research. But the reasoning behind important decisions often disappears. That may be the missing layer in how product organizations learn. A feature launches. Three months later, someone asks a simple question: “Did it work?” Analytics can tell us what happened. Jira can tell us what shipped. Research can tell us what customers said. But another question is often surprisingly difficult to answer: Why did we believe this was the right decision in the first place? What evidence did we have? What assumptions were we making? What outcome did we expect? How confident were we? And what evidence would have changed our mind? I’ve encountered versions of this problem repeatedly in product work. The decision happens. The feature ships. The team moves on. A few months later, the outcome is visible, but much of the reasoning that produced the decision has disappeared. We are getting increasingly good at remembering what happened . We are much worse at remembering what we believed before it happened . The missing record between evidence and outcome Imagine a team sees significant drop-off during onboarding. The evidence suggests one step is creating friction, so the team decides to simplify it. At decision time: Problem: New users are dropping during onboarding Evidence: Drop-off is concentrated at one step Decision: Simplify that step Assumption: Friction is the primary cause Expected outcome: Activation improves by 4% Confidence: Medium What would change our mind? No meaningful improvement in the affected cohort Preserving this changes what becomes possible later. I think of it as a Decision Receipt . Not another requirements document. Not a retrospective justification for a decision we’ve already made. Just a small, immutable record of what the team knew, assumed and expected at the moment it made the decision. Press enter or click to view image in full size A working Decision Receipt from my Product OS experiment. The expected outcome, assumptions, confidence and what would change the decision are preserved before the outcome is known. Example from an experiment I’m building: preserving the evidence, assumptions, expected outcome, confidence, contradictory evidence and what would change the decision before the outcome is known. Then reality arrives Suppose three months pass. Activation improves. But instead of the expected +4% , the actual improvement is +2.3% . Most teams would probably call that a positive result and move on. And perhaps it is. But preserving the original prediction gives us another question: Why were we wrong by 1.7 percentage points? Maybe the assumption was only partially right. Maybe one customer segment improved while another didn’t. Maybe something else changed at the same time. Maybe our confidence was too high. Maybe we predicted the direction correctly but misunderstood the magnitude. The interesting information is no longer only: Expected → Actual It is the gap between them and what that gap tells us about the assumptions behind the decision. Press enter or click to view image in full size A working Expected vs Actual review from my Product OS experiment. The original prediction remains preserved while the actual outcome, prediction gap and learning are appended — without treating observed change as causal proof. Measuring the outcome is useful. Comparing it with what we predicted lets us examine the quality of the original reasoning. Don’t rewrite the prediction after seeing the answer This part matters. If the team expected +4%, preserve +4%. Don’t quietly turn it into: “We expected activation to improve.” after discovering the result was +2.3%. Once we know what happened, the outcome often feels more predictable than it really was. Hindsight has a way of making yesterday’s uncertainty disappear. A Decision Receipt gives hindsight something to be checked against: This is what we believed before we knew the answer. The assumptions may matter more than the decision Underneath many product decisions are assumptions. Users are dropping because the journey is confusing. This segment values convenience more than price. Increasing visibility will increase adoption. Customers who try the feature once will come back. The behaviour will continue after the promotion ends. We rarely ship an assumption directly. We ship a feature, experiment, pricing change, journey or experience built on top of assumptions . That means an outcome can tell us more than whether a feature succeeded. It can tell us whether an assumption survived contact with reality. That is why I’ve started thinking that assumptions deserve their own lifecycle. Evidence can strengthen them. Contradictory evidence can weaken them. Some assumptions matter far more than others. And before committing to a decision, we should be able to ask: Which assumption would hurt us most if we’re wrong — and how uncertain are we about it? Experiments and outcomes can then validate or invalidate those assumptions. But the assumption that existed when the decision was made should remain preserved.
